claim: Myog-/- zebrafish are viable, in contrast to mice.
source: In contrast to mice, myog-/-zebrafish are viable, but have hypotrophic muscles.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by the viability of adult myog-/- fish described throughout the manuscript.

claim: Myog-/- zebrafish have hypotrophic muscles.
source: In contrast to mice, myog-/-zebrafish are viable, but have hypotrophic muscles.
evidence: Stated in abstract and demonstrated by morphometric analysis throughout the manuscript.

claim: Myog-/- myofibres have severely reduced nuclear number.
source: By isolating adult myofibres with associated MuSCs, we found that myog-/- myofibres have severely reduced nuclear number, but increased myonuclear domain size.
evidence: Stated in abstract and quantified in Figure 1G,H showing fourfold reduction in nuclei per unit length and 90% reduction in total nuclei per myofibre.

claim: Myog-/- myofibres have increased myonuclear domain size.
source: By isolating adult myofibres with associated MuSCs, we found that myog-/- myofibres have severely reduced nuclear number, but increased myonuclear domain size.
evidence: Stated in abstract and quantified in Figure 1J showing twofold increase in nuclear domain.

claim: Expression of fusogenic genes is decreased in myog-/- muscle.
source: Expression of fusogenic genes is decreased, Pax7 upregulated, MuSCs are fivefold more numerous and mis-positioned throughout the length of myog-/-myofibres instead of localising at myofibre ends as in wild-type.
evidence: Stated in abstract and shown in Figure 1B with mymk, mymx, and mrf4 mRNA downregulation.

claim: Pax7 is upregulated in myog-/- muscle.
source: Expression of fusogenic genes is decreased, Pax7 upregulated, MuSCs are fivefold more numerous and mis-positioned throughout the length of myog-/-myofibres instead of localising at myofibre ends as in wild-type.
evidence: Stated in abstract and shown in Figure 2A with pax7a and pax7b mRNA upregulation.

claim: MuSCs are fivefold more numerous in myog-/- myofibres.
source: Expression of fusogenic genes is decreased, Pax7 upregulated, MuSCs are fivefold more numerous and mis-positioned throughout the length of myog-/-myofibres instead of localising at myofibre ends as in wild-type.
evidence: Stated in abstract and shown in Figure 2E with quantification of GFP+ve cells per myofibre.

claim: MuSCs are mis-positioned throughout the length of myog-/- myofibres instead of localising at myofibre ends as in wild-type.
source: Expression of fusogenic genes is decreased, Pax7 upregulated, MuSCs are fivefold more numerous and mis-positioned throughout the length of myog-/-myofibres instead of localising at myofibre ends as in wild-type.
evidence: Stated in abstract and shown in Figure 2H,I,J demonstrating random distribution of MuSCs in myog-/- versus end-localization in wild-type.

claim: Loss of Myog dysregulates mTORC1 signalling.
source: Loss of Myog dysregulates mTORC1 signalling, resulting in an 'alerted' state of MuSCs, which display precocious activation and faster cell cycle entry ex vivo, concomitant with myod upregulation.
evidence: Stated in abstract and demonstrated in Figure 3 showing increased pRPS6 and decreased tsc1a/b expression.

claim: Myog-/- MuSCs display precocious activation and faster cell cycle entry ex vivo.
source: Loss of Myog dysregulates mTORC1 signalling, resulting in an 'alerted' state of MuSCs, which display precocious activation and faster cell cycle entry ex vivo, concomitant with myod upregulation.
evidence: Stated in abstract and shown in Figure 4E,F with EdU incorporation analysis showing 60% EdU+ve cells at day 2 in myog-/- versus 20% in sibs.

claim: Myog-/- MuSCs show myod upregulation.
source: Loss of Myog dysregulates mTORC1 signalling, resulting in an 'alerted' state of MuSCs, which display precocious activation and faster cell cycle entry ex vivo, concomitant with myod upregulation.
evidence: Stated in abstract and shown in Figure 4G with fifteenfold increase in myod mRNA in myog-/- MPCs at day 2.

claim: Myog influences the MuSC:niche relationship.
source: Thus, beyond controlling myocyte fusion, Myog influences the MuSC:niche relationship, demonstrating a multi-level contribution to muscle homeostasis throughout life.
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by data showing altered MuSC positioning, number, and activation state.

claim: Myog demonstrates a multi-level contribution to muscle homeostasis throughout life.
source: Thus, beyond controlling myocyte fusion, Myog influences the MuSC:niche relationship, demonstrating a multi-level contribution to muscle homeostasis throughout life.
evidence: Stated in abstract as a conclusion from the collective findings.

claim: Adult vertebrate muscle contains MuSCs located between the basal lamina and sarcolemma of most adult myofibres.
source: To facilitate this homeostasis, adult vertebrate muscle contains a specialised population of precursors cells, muscle stem cells (MuSCs), also termed satellite cells, located between the basal lamina and sarcolemma of most adult myofibres (Mauro, 1961).
evidence: Stated in introduction with citation to Mauro, 1961.

claim: MuSCs are mitotically dormant in normal circumstances but poised to respond to functional demand for new myonuclei throughout adult life.
source: Like other stem cells, MuSCs are mitotically dormant in normal circumstances but poised to respond to functional demand for new myonuclei throughout adult life (Relaix and Zammit, 2012; Purohit and Dhawan, 2019).
evidence: Stated in introduction with citations to Relaix and Zammit, 2012; Purohit and Dhawan, 2019.

claim: Pax7 is considered a canonical quiescent MuSC marker across several vertebrate species.
source: The transcription factor Pax7 is considered a canonical quiescent MuSC marker across several vertebrate species and its expression is maintained during the progression to activation and proliferation, before downregulation at the onset of myogenic differentiation (Berberoglu et al., 2017; Buckingham and Relaix, 2015; Chen et al., 2006; Hammond et al., 2007; Hollway et al., 2007; Kawakami et al., 1997; Seale et al., 2000; Seger et al., 2011; Zammit et al., 2006; Olguin and Olwin, 2004).
evidence: Stated in introduction with multiple citations.

claim: Pax7 expression is maintained during the progression to activation and proliferation, before downregulation at the onset of myogenic differentiation.
source: The transcription factor Pax7 is considered a canonical quiescent MuSC marker across several vertebrate species and its expression is maintained during the progression to activation and proliferation, before downregulation at the onset of myogenic differentiation (Berberoglu et al., 2017; Buckingham and Relaix, 2015; Chen et al., 2006; Hammond et al., 2007; Hollway et al., 2007; Kawakami et al., 1997; Seale et al., 2000; Seger et al., 2011; Zammit et al., 2006; Olguin and Olwin, 2004).
evidence: Stated in introduction with multiple citations.

claim: Null mutations for Pax7 severely affect MuSC maintenance and muscle regeneration in amniotes, amphibia and teleosts.
source: Null mutations for Pax7 severely affects MuSC maintenance and muscle regeneration in amniotes, amphibia and teleosts (Berberoglu et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2006; Oustanina et al., 2004; Relaix et al., 2006; Seale et al., 2000).
evidence: Stated in introduction with citations.

claim: In adult zebrafish, Pax7+ MuSCs contribute to regeneration of myofibres upon muscle damage.
source: In adult zebrafish, Pax7+ MuSCs contribute to regeneration of myofibres upon muscle damage, being the functional counterparts of MuSCs in mammals (Berberoglu et al., 2017; Hollway et al., 2007; Pipalia et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated in introduction with citations.

claim: Proper function of the MuSC pool depends on a dynamic balance between quiescence and activation and is sustained by feedback signalling from surrounding muscle.
source: Proper function of the MuSC pool depends on a dynamic balance between quiescence and activation and is sustained by feedback signalling from surrounding muscle (Mashinchian et al., 2018; Forcina et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated in introduction with citations.

claim: Myod and Myf5 are mainly expressed in MuSC and are crucial for efficient activation and proliferation.
source: In adult muscle, Myod and Myf5 are mainly expressed in MuSC and are crucial for efficient activation and proliferation (Cooper et al., 1999; Kuang et al., 2007; Megeney et al., 1996; Soleimani et al., 2012), whereas Mrf4 accumulates in mature myofibres and contributes to ensure their homeostatic size regulation (Moretti et al., 2016; Voytik et al., 1993).
evidence: Stated in introduction with citations.

claim: Mrf4 accumulates in mature myofibres and contributes to ensure their homeostatic size regulation.
source: In adult muscle, Myod and Myf5 are mainly expressed in MuSC and are crucial for efficient activation and proliferation (Cooper et al., 1999; Kuang et al., 2007; Megeney et al., 1996; Soleimani et al., 2012), whereas Mrf4 accumulates in mature myofibres and contributes to ensure their homeostatic size regulation (Moretti et al., 2016; Voytik et al., 1993).
evidence: Stated in introduction with citations.

claim: Knockout of the Myog gene in mouse leads to severe muscle deficiencies and is neonatal lethal.
source: Knockout of the Myog gene in mouse leads to severe muscle deficiencies and, in contrast to the other MRFs, is neonatal lethal (Hasty et al., 1993; Nabeshima et al., 1993), thus making it difficult to investigate Myog function in detail.
evidence: Stated in introduction with citations.

claim: Myog expression is upregulated in proliferating MuSCs that then rapidly undergo myogenic differentiation.
source: As in embryogenesis, Myog expression is upregulated in proliferating MuSCs that then rapidly undergo myogenic differentiation (Zammit et al., 2004) and its expression appears reciprocally balanced with that of Pax7 (Olguin et al., 2007; Riuzzi et al., 2014; Zammit et al., 2006; Olguin and Olwin, 2004).
evidence: Stated in introduction with citations.

claim: Myog expression appears reciprocally balanced with that of Pax7.
source: As in embryogenesis, Myog expression is upregulated in proliferating MuSCs that then rapidly undergo myogenic differentiation (Zammit et al., 2004) and its expression appears reciprocally balanced with that of Pax7 (Olguin et al., 2007; Riuzzi et al., 2014; Zammit et al., 2006; Olguin and Olwin, 2004).
evidence: Stated in introduction with citations.

claim: Depletion of mouse Myog in myoblasts does not block accumulation of differentiation markers in vitro.
source: However, depletion of mouse Myog in myoblasts does not block accumulation of differentiation markers in vitro, but cell biological aspects such as myotube formation were not explored (Meadows et al., 2008).
evidence: Stated in introduction with citation.

claim: Despite being dispensable for myogenic differentiation, Myog is essential for most myocyte fusion and its functional depletion leads to formation of mononucleated myofibres and reduced myotome growth during zebrafish embryonic/larval stages.
source: We recently expanded this observation, reporting that, despite being dispensable for myogenic differentiation, Myog is essential for most myocyte fusion and its functional depletion leads to formation of mononucleated myofibres and reduced myotome growth during zebrafish embryonic/larval stages (Ganassi et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated in introduction with citation to authors' previous work.

claim: Modulation of rodent Myog expression shifts muscle enzyme activity towards oxidative metabolism.
source: Moreover, modulation of rodent Myog expression shifts muscle enzyme activity towards oxidative metabolism, alters exercise capacity and is required for neurogenic atrophy (Flynn et al., 2010; Meadows et al., 2008; Moresi et al., 2010; Ekmark et al., 2003; Hughes et al., 1999), suggesting a broad Myog role in regulating adult muscle homeostasis.
evidence: Stated in introduction with citations.

claim: Modulation of rodent Myog expression alters exercise capacity.
source: Moreover, modulation of rodent Myog expression shifts muscle enzyme activity towards oxidative metabolism, alters exercise capacity and is required for neurogenic atrophy (Flynn et al., 2010; Meadows et al., 2008; Moresi et al., 2010; Ekmark et al., 2003; Hughes et al., 1999), suggesting a broad Myog role in regulating adult muscle homeostasis.
evidence: Stated in introduction with citations.

claim: Myog is required for neurogenic atrophy.
source: Moreover, modulation of rodent Myog expression shifts muscle enzyme activity towards oxidative metabolism, alters exercise capacity and is required for neurogenic atrophy (Flynn et al., 2010; Meadows et al., 2008; Moresi et al., 2010; Ekmark et al., 2003; Hughes et al., 1999), suggesting a broad Myog role in regulating adult muscle homeostasis.
evidence: Stated in introduction with citations.

claim: Almost complete depletion of mouse Myog after birth results in decreased muscle size.
source: Congruent with the fish phenotype, almost complete depletion of mouse Myog after birth results in decreased muscle size (Knapp et al., 2006; Meadows et al., 2008), thereby confirming a conserved vertebrate role for Myog in regulating bulk muscle growth and maintenance.
evidence: Stated in introduction with citations.

claim: Gene expression analysis on dissected adult trunk muscle confirmed continued significant downregulation of myog mRNA in myog-/- fish compared to co-reared sib controls.
source: Gene expression analysis on dissected adult trunk muscle confirmed continued significant downregulation of myog mRNA in myog-/- fish compared to co-reared sib controls (Figure 1A,B) in line with the nonsense-mediated decay reported previously (Ganassi et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 1B showing qPCR data.

claim: Levels of mRNA encoded by the terminal myogenesis genes mymk (tmem8c), mymx and mrf4 (myf6) were downregulated by 52%, 38% and 68%, respectively, in myog-/- compare to the relative expression in sib.
source: Levels of mRNA encoded by the terminal myogenesis genes mymk (tmem8c), mymx and mrf4 (myf6) were downregulated by 52%, 38% and 68%, respectively, in myog-/- compare to the relative expression in sib, as during the embryonic stage, suggesting a continuous muscle defect in adulthood (Figure 1B).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 1B showing qPCR data.

claim: Both juvenile and adult mutant myofibres were on average 20% and 50% shorter than those in control, respectively.
source: Both juvenile and adult mutant myofibres were on average 20% and 50% shorter than those in control, respectively, demonstrating an early onset growth deficit in myog-/-, with lifecourse worsening (Figure 1C,D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 1C,D showing myofibre length measurements.

claim: Sarcomere length was unaffected in adult myog-/- myofibres.
source: Despite significant 50% reduction in overall fibre length, sarcomere length was unaffected in adult myog-/- myofibres, as in embryonic myofibres (Figure 1E; Ganassi et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 1E showing sarcomere length measurements.

claim: Myofibres isolated from the adult hypomorphic myogfh265 mutants were indistinguishable from those of age-matched sibs.
source: In contrast, myofibres isolated from the adult hypomorphic myogfh265 mutants (Hinits et al., 2011; Ganassi et al., 2018) were indistinguishable from those of age-matched sibs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Nuclear numbers per unit length were reduced fourfold in myog-/- mutants.
source: Indeed, nuclear numbers per unit length were reduced fourfold in mutants (Figure 1G).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 1G showing quantification.

claim: The average number of nuclei associated with each adult myofibre was reduced from an average of 95 nuclei per myofibre in sibs to nearly 12 nuclei per myofibre in myog-/-.
source: Congruently, calculation of the average number of nuclei associated with each adult myofibre by multiplying the number of nuclei/unit length by the length revealed an approximate 90% reduction, from an average of 95 nuclei per myofibre in sibs to nearly 12 nuclei per myofibre in myog-/- (Figure 1H).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 1H showing quantification.

claim: Juvenile sib myofibres had significantly more nuclei than adult myog-/- myofibres.
source: Juvenile sib myofibres had significantly more nuclei than adult myog-/- myofibres, confirming ongoing myonuclear accretion defect in myog-/- (Figure 1G,H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 1G,H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Lack of Myog led to an average persistent decrease of 40% in myofibre diameter.
source: Further morphometric analysis revealed that lack of Myog led to an average persistent decrease of 40% in myofibre diameter resulting in 50% reduction of myofibre surface area, compared to age-matched juvenile and adult sib, respectively (Figure 1F,I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 1F,I showing quantification.

claim: Lack of Myog resulted in 50% reduction of myofibre surface area.
source: Further morphometric analysis revealed that lack of Myog led to an average persistent decrease of 40% in myofibre diameter resulting in 50% reduction of myofibre surface area, compared to age-matched juvenile and adult sib, respectively (Figure 1F,I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 1F,I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The volume and surface area per fibre-associated nucleus (nuclear domain and surface area domain size (SADS), respectively) were increased by almost twofold and threefold, respectively, in myog-/-.
source: Indeed, as expected, both the volume and surface area per fibre-associated nucleus (nuclear domain and surface area domain size (SADS), respectively) were increased by almost twofold and threefold, respectively, in myog-/- (Figure 1J and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F) indicating both inadequate nuclear accretion, congruent with suppression of mymk and mymx mRNAs (Figure 1B), and a compensatory increase in nuclear domain and SADS, which remained larger in mutants throughout life, showing no sign of return to a normal size with time.
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 1J and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Both genotypes displayed significant increase in both myofibre diameter, surface area (SA) and number of nuclei between juvenile and adult stages, indicating ongoing muscle growth.
source: Nevertheless, both genotypes displayed significant increase in both myofibre diameter, surface area (SA) and number of nuclei between juvenile and adult stages, indicating ongoing muscle growth (Figure 1G,I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 1G,I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Although myofibre SA and number of nuclei positively correlated in myog-/-, there was reduced nuclear accretion as myofibres acquired larger area compared to sib, highlighting a significantly different growth mode between the two genotypes.
source: However, although myofibre SA and number of nuclei positively correlated in myog-/-, we observed a reduced nuclear accretion as myofibres acquired larger area compared to sib, hence highlighting a significantly different growth mode between the two genotypes (different trend slopes) (Figure 1K).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 1K showing growth mode analysis.

claim: The incremental increase in myofibre SA over the juvenile-to-adult time-frame was significantly reduced in myog-/-.
source: Coherently, the incremental increase in myofibre SA over the juvenile-to-adult time-frame was significantly reduced in myog-/-, confirming a persistent deficit in muscle growth (Figure 1L).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 1L.

claim: Gene expression analysis on whole muscle showed upregulation of pax7a and pax7b mRNAs of 82% and 120%, respectively, in myog-/- compared to control sibs.
source: Gene expression analysis on whole muscle showed upregulation of pax7a and pax7b mRNAs of 82% and 120%, respectively, in myog-/- compared to control sibs, but no change in pax3a or pax3b (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 2A showing qPCR data.

claim: There was no change in pax3a or pax3b expression in myog-/- compared to control sibs.
source: Gene expression analysis on whole muscle showed upregulation of pax7a and pax7b mRNAs of 82% and 120%, respectively, in myog-/- compared to control sibs, but no change in pax3a or pax3b (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Myf5 mRNA was upregulated by over 200% in myog-/- muscle.
source: Myf5 mRNA, a marker of partially-activated or 'alerted' MuSCs in mice and MPCs in fish, and known to be a Pax7 target gene (Coutelle et al., 2001; Kuang et al., 2007; Soleimani et al., 2012), was upregulated by over 200%, further suggesting an increase of MuSCs number in myog-/-.
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 2A showing qPCR data.

claim: Myod mRNA was unaltered in myog-/- muscle.
source: In contrast, myod mRNA, a marker of fully-activated proliferating MuSCs (Zammit et al., 2004; Zammit et al., 2002; Megeney et al., 1996), was unaltered (Figure 2A).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 2A showing qPCR data.

claim: Immunostaining of GFP-positive (GFP+ve) cells with the DP312 antibody revealed co-labelling of virtually all GFP+ve cells, confirming MuSC identity.
source: Immunostaining of GFP-positive (GFP+ve) cells with the DP312 antibody, that recognises fish Pax3/Pax7 (Hammond et al., 2007; Davis et al., 2005), revealed co-labelling of virtually all GFP+ve cells, thus confirming MuSC identity (Figure 2D).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 2D showing immunostaining data.

claim: Single myog-/- myofibres bore around five GFP+ve cells on average, compared to only one on sib myofibres.
source: Upon muscle dissociation, we observed that single myog-/- myofibres bore around five GFP+ve cells on average, compared to only one on sib myofibres (Figure 2E).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 2E showing quantification.

claim: Almost 40% of nuclei associated with myog-/- myofibres were in GFP+ve cells compared to less than 2% in sib.
source: Indeed, almost 40% of nuclei associated with myog-/- myofibres were in GFP+ve cells compared to less than 2% in sib (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Sib myofibres have over thirteenfold more genuine myofibre nuclei (i.e. myonuclei) than myog-/- myofibres.
source: Subtraction of MuSC nuclei from the total nuclei associated with isolated adult myofibres, revealed that sib myofibres have over thirteenfold more genuine myofibre nuclei (i.e. myonuclei) than myog-/- myofibres (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The myonuclear domain was increased by 2.3-fold in myog-/- fibres.
source: In line with SADS, the myonuclear domain was increased by 2.3-fold in myog-/- fibres (Figure 2F), despite the eightfold reduction in absolute myofibre volume (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 2F showing quantification.

claim: In control sib, MuSCs were found mostly localised close to the myofibre end, whereas in myog-/- the supernumerary MuSCs were randomly distributed along the myofibre length.
source: In control sib, MuSCs were found mostly localised close to the myofibre end, whereas in myog-/- the supernumerary MuSCs were randomly distributed along the myofibre length (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: In sibs, 70% of myofibres had a single associated MuSC, which was usually within 20 µm from the myofibre end.
source: In sibs, 70% of myofibres had a single associated MuSC, which was usually within 20 µm from the myofibre end (Figure 2G,I,J and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 2G,I,J and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G,H.

claim: Only 33% of myog-/- myofibres had a single MuSC.
source: In contrast, only 33% of myofibres had a single MuSC in mutants (Figure 2G,I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G,H), which displayed consistent random location, often far from the myofibre end (Figure 2I,J).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 2G,I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G,H.

claim: Around 60% of myog-/- myofibres bore two or more MuSCs, whereas only 9% of sib myofibres had two or more MuSCs.
source: Around 60% of myog-/- myofibres bore two or more MuSCs, whereas only 9% of sib myofibres had two or more MuSCs, and none had over three (Figure 2G).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 2G.

claim: 21% of sib myofibres had no GFP+ve cells, compared to only 5% of myog-/- myofibres.
source: Strikingly, 21% of sib myofibres had no GFP+ve cells, compared to only 5% of myog-/- myofibres (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Whole muscle analysis revealed 130% increased level of igf1 mRNA in myog-/-.
source: Whole muscle analysis revealed 130% increased level of igf1 mRNA and nearly 50% downregulation of myostatin b (mstnb) mRNA, both regulators of muscle growth and the mTORC1 (mechanistic Target Of Rapamycin Complex 1) pathway (Yoon, 2017; Trendelenburg et al., 2009), suggesting that lack of Myog triggers a growth signalling response (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 3B showing qPCR data.

claim: Whole muscle analysis revealed nearly 50% downregulation of myostatin b (mstnb) mRNA in myog-/-.
source: Whole muscle analysis revealed 130% increased level of igf1 mRNA and nearly 50% downregulation of myostatin b (mstnb) mRNA, both regulators of muscle growth and the mTORC1 (mechanistic Target Of Rapamycin Complex 1) pathway (Yoon, 2017; Trendelenburg et al., 2009), suggesting that lack of Myog triggers a growth signalling response (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 3B showing qPCR data.

claim: Expression of the zebrafish IGF1 receptors, igfr1a and igfr1b was unaltered in myog-/-.
source: In contrast, expression of the zebrafish IGF1 receptors, igfr1a and igfr1b was unaltered (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) indicating that myog-/- myofibres, and/or MuSCs, may respond to the higher IGF1 level similarly to sib.
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Western blot analysis of whole muscle extracts revealed that whereas AKT phosphorylation at Ser473 (pAKT) appeared unchanged, downstream phosphorylation of RPS6 at Ser240/244 (pRPS6) was enhanced fourfold in myog-/- muscle compared to sib.
source: Western blot analysis of whole muscle extracts revealed that whereas AKT phosphorylation at Ser473 (pAKT) appeared unchanged, downstream phosphorylation of RPS6 at Ser240/244 (pRPS6) was enhanced fourfold in myog-/- muscle compared to sib (Figure 3D).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 3D showing Western blot data.

claim: Myog-/- MuSCs showed a robust twofold increase in pRPS6 level.
source: Myog-/- MuSCs showed a robust twofold increase in pRPS6 level (Figure 3E,F), in line with quantification in whole muscle.
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 3E,F showing immunostaining quantification.

claim: No change in pRPS6 was detected in myofibres themselves.
source: No change was detected in myofibres themselves.
evidence: Stated in results following analysis of pRPS6 in MuSCs.

claim: Levels of tsc1a and tsc1b mRNAs were reduced by 51% and 57%, respectively, in myog-/- muscle.
source: Levels of tsc1a and tsc1b mRNAs were reduced by 51% and 57%, respectively, in myog-/- muscle, whereas tsc2 mRNA was unchanged compare to sib (Figure 3G), consistent with increased pRPS6.
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 3G showing qPCR data.

claim: tsc2 mRNA was unchanged in myog-/- muscle compared to sib.
source: Levels of tsc1a and tsc1b mRNAs were reduced by 51% and 57%, respectively, in myog-/- muscle, whereas tsc2 mRNA was unchanged compare to sib (Figure 3G), consistent with increased pRPS6.
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 3G showing qPCR data.

claim: Myog-/- mutants yielded at least three times as many mononucleate cells than did sibs after 4 days in culture.
source: Myog-/- mutants yielded at least three times as many mononucleate cells than did sibs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), paralleling the increased number of MuSCs on freshly-isolated myofibres.
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The vast majority (80–90%) of cells from fish of either genotype was GFP+ve, so bona fide MPCs.
source: The vast majority (80–90%) of cells from fish of either genotype was GFP+ve, so bona fide MPCs.
evidence: Stated in results following culture of myofibres.

claim: Myog-/- myofibres displayed an average threefold increased GFP+ve cell yield compared to sibs.
source: Myog-/- myofibres also displayed an average threefold increased GFP+ve cell yield compared to sibs (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 4A–C.

claim: Sib myofibres yielded around 40 MPCs within the 4-day culture period, reflecting a mean doubling time of around 20 hr.
source: Within the 4-day culture period, sib myofibres (70% of which had only a single GFP+ve MuSC) yielded around 40 MPCs, reflecting a mean doubling time of around 20 hr.
evidence: Stated in results with calculation based on culture data.

claim: All cells immunoreacted for Desmin, confirming their myogenic identity.
source: Importantly, although both genotypes yielded a GFP-ve cell population, all cells immunoreacted for Desmin, confirming their myogenic identity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1A showing immunostaining.

claim: The relative MPC proliferation rates were not significantly different among genotypes.
source: Notably, the relative MPC proliferation rates were not significantly different among genotypes, calculated as the ratio of the number of GFP+ve MPCs obtained after 4 days in culture to the average number of GFP+ve MuSC per myofibre at the time of isolation (Figure 4D).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 4D showing calculation.

claim: An EdU pulse 2 days after plating revealed that 60% of myog-/- MPCs were EdU+ve, compared to only 20% of sib MPCs.
source: An EdU pulse 2 days after plating revealed striking differences between myog-/- MPCs, 60% of which were EdU+ve, compared to sib MPCs, only 20% of which incorporated EdU (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 4E,F showing EdU incorporation data.

claim: On day 3, sib MPCs were almost 60% EdU+ve, whereas incorporation into myog-/- MPCs was significantly reduced compared to both sibs on day 3 and myog-/- MPCs on day 2.
source: A day later (on day 3), the difference in proliferation had reversed; sib MPCs were almost 60% EdU+ve, whereas incorporation into myog-/- MPCs was significantly reduced compared to both sibs on day 3 and myog-/- MPCs on day 2 (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 4E,F showing EdU incorporation data.

claim: Statistical analysis of overall EdU incorporation dynamics as Area Under Curve (AUC) revealed slightly higher proliferation rate of sib MPCs.
source: Statistical analysis of overall EdU incorporation dynamics as Area Under Curve (AUC) revealed slightly higher proliferation rate of sib MPCs (Figure 4E).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 4E showing AUC analysis.

claim: Both pax7a and pax7b were more abundant, fourfold and threefold, respectively, in myog-/- MPCs at 2 days compared to sib.
source: Both pax7a and pax7b were more abundant, fourfold and threefold, respectively, in myog-/- MPCs at 2 days compared to sib (Figure 4G), consistent with the higher percentage of MuSCs observed (Figure 4C).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 4G showing qPCR data.

claim: While pax7a mRNA reduced with time, pax7b mRNA was maintained at similar level between day 2 and day 3 across genotypes.
source: Strikingly, while pax7a mRNA reduced with time, pax7b mRNA was maintained at similar level between day 2 and day 3 across genotypes, despite confirming overall increased level in myog-/- MPCs (Figure 4G).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 4G showing qPCR data.

claim: myod mRNA was fifteenfold more abundant in myog-/- MPCs compared to sib.
source: Moreover, myod mRNA was fifteenfold more abundant in myog-/- MPCs compared to sib, again suggesting an earlier entry into activation phase.
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 4G showing qPCR data.

claim: Higher myod expression in myog-/- MPCs lasted into day 3.
source: Notably, higher myod expression in myog-/- MPCs lasted into day 3.
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 4G showing qPCR data.

claim: myf5 mRNA level appeared similar in myog-/- and sib MPCs at both 2 and 3 days.
source: In contrast, myf5 mRNA level appeared similar in myog-/- and sib MPCs at both 2 and 3 days, although tending to decrease at the later timepoint in sibs (Figure 4G), perhaps reflecting their slower activation.
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 4G showing qPCR data.

claim: Expression of mef2d, mylpfa, flnca and mybpc1 mRNAs was significantly higher in myog-/- relative to sib MPCs on day 3.
source: We assessed onset of differentiation by analysing expression of mef2d, mylpfa (encoding a fast myosin light chain), flnca and mybpc1, crucial players in myogenesis, which revealed significantly higher levels of all the assessed mRNAs in myog-/- relative to sib MPCs on day 3, with an approximate upregulation of mef2d (twofold), mylpfa (fortyfold), flnca (fivefold) and mybpc1 (thirtyfold) (Figure 4H).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 4H showing qPCR data.

claim: Only mylpfa showed accumulation in myog-/- MPCs already at day 2.
source: Among the four, only mylpfa showed accumulation in myog-/- MPCs already at day 2.
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 4H showing qPCR data.

claim: Mutant MPCs significantly accumulated cdkn1a (p21) mRNA (fourfold) between day 2 and day 3.
source: In addition, mutant MPCs significantly accumulated cdkn1a (p21) mRNA (fourfold) between day 2 and day 3, in line with reduced proliferation and myogenic progression, whereas sib MPCs did not (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1D showing qPCR data.

claim: Level of cdkn1ca (p57) was unaltered in both myog-/- and sib MPCs.
source: In contrast, level of cdkn1ca (p57), which promotes terminal myogenesis (Osborn et al., 2011), was unaltered in both myog-/- and sib MPCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), highlighting the immature state of myogenic progression.
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1D showing qPCR data.

claim: Immunostaining confirmed accumulation of sarcomeric myosin heavy chain (MyHC) and significantly higher differentiation index in myog-/- compared to sib MPCs at day 3.
source: However, despite the continued exposure to growth medium, immunostaining confirmed accumulation of sarcomeric myosin heavy chain (MyHC) and significantly higher differentiation index in myog-/- compared to sib MPCs at day 3, (Figure 4I).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 4I showing immunostaining and quantification.

claim: Upon culture under differentiation conditions, sib MPCs underwent cell fusion forming visible multinucleated myotubes, whereas differentiated myog-/- MPCs remained mostly mononucleated.
source: As reported previously (Ganassi et al., 2018), upon culture under differentiation conditions, sib MPCs underwent cell fusion forming visible multinucleated myotubes, whereas differentiated myog-/- MPCs remained mostly mononucleated (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Stated in results with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1E showing immunostaining.

claim: Myog function is dispensable for MPC proliferation and terminal differentiation.
source: Altogether, our data indicate that whereas Myog function is dispensable for MPC proliferation and terminal differentiation, its lack either prevents MuSCs achieving full quiescence or accelerates MuSC transition into the proliferation phase, suggesting that Myog contributes to maintaining the MuSC niche.
evidence: Stated in results as a conclusion from the culture experiments.

claim: Lack of Myog either prevents MuSCs achieving full quiescence or accelerates MuSC transition into the proliferation phase.
source: Altogether, our data indicate that whereas Myog function is dispensable for MPC proliferation and terminal differentiation, its lack either prevents MuSCs achieving full quiescence or accelerates MuSC transition into the proliferation phase, suggesting that Myog contributes to maintaining the MuSC niche.
evidence: Stated in results as a conclusion from the culture experiments.

claim: Myog contributes to maintaining the MuSC niche.
source: Altogether, our data indicate that whereas Myog function is dispensable for MPC proliferation and terminal differentiation, its lack either prevents MuSCs achieving full quiescence or accelerates MuSC transition into the proliferation phase, suggesting that Myog contributes to maintaining the MuSC niche.
evidence: Stated in results as a conclusion from the culture experiments.

claim: Total number of Pax7+ MuSCs is increased around 10-fold in adult myog-/- mutant myotome.
source: In addition to the fivefold increase in MuSC/adult myofibre and 50% reduction in myofibre length reported here, we previously described that adult myog-/- mutants have unaltered body length and numbers of myofibre profiles/transverse body section roughly equal to their non-mutant siblings (Ganassi et al., 2018). Taken together, these data suggest that total number of Pax7+ MuSCs is increased around 10-fold in adult myog-/- mutant myotome.
evidence: Stated in discussion as a calculation based on current and previous data.

claim: In mouse, expression of Pax7 and Myog in MuSC appear to be mutually exclusive and controlled through reciprocal inhibition in in vitro studies.
source: In mouse, expression of Pax7 and Myog in MuSC appear to be mutually exclusive and controlled through reciprocal inhibition in in vitro studies (Olguin et al., 2007; Riuzzi et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated in discussion with citations.

claim: Persistent Pax7 expression delays Myog accumulation in cultured myoblasts and ex vivo in MuSCs on myofibres.
source: Persistent Pax7 expression delays Myog accumulation in cultured myoblasts and ex vivo in MuSCs on myofibres, whereas silencing of Myog can result in retention of Pax7 expression in differentiation (Olguin et al., 2007; Zammit et al., 2006).
evidence: Stated in discussion with citations.

claim: Myog is required for adult myoblast fusion in vitro.
source: As Myog is required for adult myoblast fusion in vitro (Ganassi et al., 2018) and mymk and mymx mRNAs are reduced in adult myog-/- muscle, one must consider the possibility that some pax7a:GFP+ve mononucleate cells are not MuSCs but differentiated myocytes that retain the pax7a reporter and are unable to fuse.
evidence: Stated in discussion with citation to authors' previous work.

claim: Most myog-/- MuSCs enter into S-phase after 2 days ex vivo.
source: However, we detect Pax3/7 protein in MuSCs, showing that strong GFP accumulation is not just perdurance of earlier signal. Moreover, most myog-/- MuSCs enter into S-phase after 2 days ex vivo.
evidence: Stated in discussion based on EdU incorporation data.

claim: Myog-/- MPCs quickly upregulate the differentiation marker mylpfa fortyfold.
source: Subsequently, myog-/- MPCs quickly upregulate the differentiation marker mylpfa fortyfold, suggesting that an insignificant fraction was previously terminally differentiated.
evidence: Stated in discussion based on qPCR data.

claim: Myog-/- muscle expresses more myf5, a MPC marker.
source: In addition, myog-/- muscle expresses more myf5, a MPC marker.
evidence: Stated in discussion based on qPCR data.

claim: In post-natal rodent muscle, Myf5 is expressed in MuSCs, not myofibres.
source: In post-natal rodent muscle, Myf5 is expressed in MuSCs, not myofibres (Beauchamp et al., 2000).
evidence: Stated in discussion with citation.

claim: Murine Myog-knockout led to Myf5 accumulation in neonatal limb muscle.
source: Like our finding, murine Myog-knockout also led to Myf5 accumulation in neonatal limb muscle, even though one-third of the total nuclei are still MuSCs/MPCs in wild type neonates (Cardasis and Cooper, 1975; Rawls et al., 1998).
evidence: Stated in discussion with citations.

claim: Myog-/- MPCs readily undergo differentiation in culture and during myogenesis in the embryo.
source: First, myog-/- MPCs readily undergo differentiation in culture and during myogenesis in the embryo (Ganassi et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated in discussion with citation to authors' previous work.

claim: Although muscle is reduced in size in myog-/-, there is enough formed to support life and sarcomere length is unaffected.
source: Second, although muscle is reduced in size, there is enough formed to support life and sarcomere length is unaffected, so terminal differentiation is fairly efficient without Myog during larval and adult growth and any required muscle repair.
evidence: Stated in discussion based on morphometric data.

claim: Both in fish and amniotes, MPCs ready to differentiate express high levels of Myod.
source: Third, both in fish and amniotes, MPCs ready to differentiate express high levels of Myod, which acts in a feedforward mechanism to trigger cell cycle exit and Myog expression (Weintraub et al., 1991; Hinits et al., 2009).
evidence: Stated in discussion with citations.

claim: Increased levels of myod mRNA are not observed in myog-/- mutant muscle.
source: We do not, however, observe increased levels of myod mRNA in myog-/- mutant muscle.
evidence: Stated in discussion based on qPCR data.

claim: When myog-/- MPCs are placed in culture they dramatically upregulate myod.
source: Nevertheless, when myog-/- MPCs are placed in culture they dramatically upregulate myod, arguing that Myod upregulation is also a characteristic of adult zebrafish MPC myogenic progression.
evidence: Stated in discussion based on qPCR data from cultured MPCs.

claim: Active accumulation of MuSCs is suggested by the increase in pax7a, pax7b and myf5 mRNAs in myog-/- mutant muscle.
source: Active accumulation of MuSCs, on the other hand, is suggested by the increase in pax7a, pax7b and myf5 mRNAs in myog-/- mutant muscle.
evidence: Stated in discussion based on qPCR data.

claim: In wild-type fish 21% of myofibres have no associated MuSCs, despite having around 95 myofibre nuclei.
source: In wild-type fish 21% of myofibres have no associated MuSCs, despite having around 95 myofibre nuclei.
evidence: Stated in discussion based on MuSC counting data.

claim: MuSC/MPCs must migrate across the basal lamina between fibres in order to grow or repair damage.
source: This finding strongly argues that, in order to grow or repair damage, MuSC/MPCs must migrate across the basal lamina between fibres, as occurs in developing rodent muscle (Hughes and Blau, 1990).
evidence: Stated in discussion as an inference from the data, with citation.

claim: 0.92 MuSCs/wild-type myofibre are observed on average.
source: We observe 0.92 MuSCs/wild-type myofibre, on average.
evidence: Stated in discussion based on MuSC counting data.

claim: If one assumes random MuSC distribution amongst myofibres, the Poisson distribution predicts that 40% of myofibres should have no associated-MuSCs.
source: If one assumes random MuSC distribution amongst myofibres, the Poisson distribution predicts that 40% of myofibres should have no associated-MuSCs.
evidence: Stated in discussion as a statistical calculation.

claim: The lower proportion of myofibres lacking MuSCs suggests that MuSCs are not distributed randomly.
source: The lower proportion of myofibres lacking MuSCs suggests that MuSCs are not distributed randomly.
evidence: Stated in discussion as an inference from comparing observed and expected distributions.

claim: Poissonian distribution would predict that 37% of myofibres should have a single MuSC.
source: Conversely, Poissonian distribution would predict that 37% of myofibres should have a single MuSC.
evidence: Stated in discussion as a statistical calculation.

claim: The observed value of 70% of myofibres with a single MuSC strongly suggests that MuSCs actively disperse between myofibres.
source: The observed value of 70% strongly suggests that MuSCs actively disperse between myofibres.
evidence: Stated in discussion as an inference from comparing observed and expected distributions.

claim: Around 5% of myog-/- myofibres have no associated MuSC, which is far more than expected by the Poisson distribution (1.5%).
source: Despite the fivefold increase in MuSCs in myog-/- mutant, around 5% of myofibres still have no associated MuSC, which is far more than expected by the Poisson distribution (1.5%).
evidence: Stated in discussion comparing observed and expected distributions.

claim: 33% of myog-/- myofibres with only a single MuSC compares with an expected value of 6%.
source: Similarly, the 33% of myog-/- myofibres with only a single MuSC compares with an expected value of 6%.
evidence: Stated in discussion comparing observed and expected distributions.

claim: Myog-/- myofibres with over 10 MuSCs are over-represented, perhaps due to rare local regenerative events.
source: In contrast, myog-/- myofibres with over 10 MuSCs are over-represented, perhaps due to rare local regenerative events.
evidence: Stated in discussion as an observation with speculative explanation.

claim: Myofibres in both wild-type and myog-/- mutant contain a single specific niche for MuSCs.
source: These observations raise the possibility that myofibres in both wild-type and myog-/- mutant contain a single specific niche for MuSCs.
evidence: Stated in discussion as a hypothesis based on the distribution data.

claim: Most MuSCs associated with isolated myofibres in zebrafish are located near myofibre ends.
source: Most MuSCs associated with isolated myofibres in zebrafish are located near myofibre ends, which would be attached to the vertical myoseptum tendon-like structure in vivo.
evidence: Stated in discussion based on MuSC localization data.

claim: The fibre end provides a special niche in which MuSCs accumulate, perhaps formed in association with the myotendinous junction (MTJ).
source: We hypothesise that the fibre end provides a special niche in which MuSCs accumulate, perhaps formed in association with the myotendinous junction (MTJ).
evidence: Stated in discussion as a hypothesis based on MuSC localization data.

claim: The preferred location of MuSCs in wild-type myofibres is between 10 and 20 µm from the myofibre end.
source: Strikingly, the preferred location of MuSCs in wild-type myofibres is between 10 and 20 µm from the myofibre end, suggesting that MuSCs locate not on the MTJ surface itself, but on the immediately adjacent cylindrical sarcolemma, retaining a potential physical contact with the MTJ.
evidence: Stated in discussion based on MuSC localization data.

claim: This suggested location of the MuSC niche may relate to evidence that addition of new nuclei occurs preferentially at the ends of myofibres during growth.
source: Moreover, this suggested location of the MuSC niche may relate to evidence that addition of new nuclei occurs preferentially at the ends of myofibres during growth (Kitiyakara and Angevine, 1963; Aziz and Goldspink, 1974).
evidence: Stated in discussion with citations.

claim: Upon explant ex vivo, MuSCs activate and begin to migrate away from myofibre ends.
source: Upon explant ex vivo, MuSCs activate and begin to migrate away from myofibre ends.
evidence: Stated in discussion as an observation.

claim: In myog-/- mutants, the increased number of MuSCs are almost randomly distributed along the fibre.
source: In myog-/- mutants, the increased number of MuSCs are almost randomly distributed along the fibre, but the slightly higher abundance at myofibre ends might suggest that cells disperse once the MTJ niche is filled.
evidence: Stated in discussion based on MuSC localization data.

claim: When the fraction of myofibres in myog-/- mutants that have only a single MuSC were analysed separately, significant dispersal was still observed.
source: However, when the fraction of myofibres in myog-/- mutants that have only a single MuSC were analysed separately, significant dispersal was still observed.
evidence: Stated in discussion based on MuSC localization data.

claim: Loss of MTJ contact by the short myofibres in myog-/- mutants may contribute to niche disruption.
source: An additional possibility is that loss of MTJ contact by the short myofibres in myog-/- mutants contributes to niche disruption.
evidence: Stated in discussion as a hypothesis.

claim: Myog is required for assembly of the myofibre end MuSC:niche complex.
source: We conclude that Myog is required for assembly of the myofibre end MuSC:niche complex.
evidence: Stated in discussion as a conclusion from the MuSC localization data.

claim: Mammalian MuSCs are generally not associated with myofibre ends, perhaps because myofibres are longer.
source: Mammalian MuSCs are generally not associated with myofibre ends, perhaps because myofibres are longer.
evidence: Stated in discussion as an observation with speculative explanation.

claim: Zebrafish myofibres are on average 1 mm long and rarely exceed 2 mm.
source: Zebrafish myofibres are on average 1 mm long and rarely exceed 2 mm.
evidence: Stated in discussion based on morphometric data.

claim: In murine limb muscles, myofibres are up to 1 cm long.
source: In contrast, in the murine muscles most frequently analysed, those of the limbs, myofibres are up to 1 cm long.
evidence: Stated in discussion as general knowledge.

claim: The more numerous nuclei and larger number of MuSCs required for efficient growth and repair have allowed the MuSC niche to disperse along the myofibre in mammals.
source: We suggest that the more numerous nuclei and larger number of MuSCs required for efficient growth and repair have allowed (or selected for) the MuSC niche to disperse along the myofibre.
evidence: Stated in discussion as a hypothesis.

claim: MuSCs are not increased in myog-/- mutant larvae.
source: However, MuSCs are not increased in mutant larvae (Ganassi et al., 2018) so it seems the defect worsens over the life course, suggesting a continuous need for Myog.
evidence: Stated in discussion with citation to authors' previous work.

claim: The MuSC defect in myog-/- worsens over the life course, suggesting a continuous need for Myog.
source: However, MuSCs are not increased in mutant larvae (Ganassi et al., 2018) so it seems the defect worsens over the life course, suggesting a continuous need for Myog.
evidence: Stated in discussion as an inference from comparing larval and adult data.

claim: An early study investigating differential expression of Myod and Myog in rat muscle observed rare but intense accumulation of Myog mRNA along myofibre edges, anatomically reminiscent of MuSC niche.
source: An early study investigating differential expression of Myod and Myog in rat muscle observed rare but intense accumulation of Myog mRNA along myofibre edges, anatomically reminiscent of MuSC niche (Hughes et al., 1993).
evidence: Stated in discussion with citation.

claim: Myog expression predominates in oxidative myofibres also characterised by higher MuSC density.
source: Notably, Myog expression predominates in oxidative myofibres also characterised by higher MuSC density (Gibson and Schultz, 1982; Hughes et al., 1993).
evidence: Stated in discussion with citations.

claim: Rantanen et al. identified a population of dormant Myog+ MuSCs which may contribute to muscle repair bypassing the proliferation step.
source: Rantanen et al. identified a population of dormant Myog+ MuSCs which may contribute to muscle repair bypassing the proliferation step (Rantanen et al., 1995).
evidence: Stated in discussion with citation.

claim: Co-expression of Pax7 and Myog was observed in a satellite-cell study in transverse sections of both mouse soleus and EDL muscles.
source: Co-expression of Pax7 and Myog was observed in a satellite-cell study in transverse sections of both mouse soleus and EDL muscles (Schultz et al., 2006) and in rare cells in fish dermomyotome (Devoto et al., 2006).
evidence: Stated in discussion with citations.

claim: Immunohistochemistry on human resting muscle biopsies found Myog expression in MuSC but not in myonuclei.
source: Likewise, immunohistochemistry on human resting muscle biopsies found Myog expression in MuSC but not in myonuclei (Lindström et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated in discussion with citation.

claim: The Blau group reported a low but detectable level of Myog protein in both resting murine MuSCs and in MPCs returning to quiescence after recovery from injury.
source: More recently, the Blau group reported a low but detectable level of Myog protein in both resting murine MuSCs and in MPCs returning to quiescence after recovery from injury (Porpiglia et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated in discussion with citation.

claim: Datasets show that Myog mRNA is present in quiescent MuSCs and rapidly decreases significantly during the 3 hours of myofibre isolation.
source: In addition, datasets show that Myog mRNA is present in quiescent MuSCs and rapidly decreases significantly during the 3 hours of myofibre isolation (Machado et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated in discussion with citation.

claim: Mrf4 expression in MuSC was downregulated during the 3 hours of myofibre isolation, concomitant with exit from quiescence marked by the upregulation of Myod.
source: Interestingly, Mrf4 expression in MuSC was downregulated in the same time frame, concomitant with exit from quiescence marked by the upregulation of Myod, demonstrating the presence of two well-known muscle 'differentiation-specific' markers in dormant stem cells.
evidence: Stated in discussion with reference to datasets.

claim: MRFs including Myog are required in the adult to restrict murine myofibre size.
source: MRFs including Myog are required in the adult to restrict murine myofibre size (Moresi et al., 2010; Moretti et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated in discussion with citations.

claim: In zebrafish, Myog is required both for myocyte fusion that permits increase in nuclear number and consequent growth to the normal fibre size.
source: We find that, in zebrafish, Myog is required both for myocyte fusion that permits increase in nuclear number and consequent growth to the normal fibre size.
evidence: Stated in discussion as a conclusion from the current study.

claim: Myog limits myonuclear domain size both in juvenile and adult muscle.
source: We also show that Myog limits myonuclear domain size both in juvenile and adult muscle.
evidence: Stated in discussion as a conclusion from the current study.

claim: Conditional depletion of Myog in adult mouse muscle decreased myofibre cross-sectional area.
source: Conditional depletion of Myog in adult mouse muscle decreased myofibre cross-sectional area, although further morphometric analysis of myofibre nuclear domains was not reported (Meadows et al., 2008).
evidence: Stated in discussion with citation.

claim: In addition to its role in promoting MPC differentiation and fusion, Myog restricts the volume of sarcoplasm supported by each myonucleus, both in denervated and innervated adult muscle.
source: It therefore seems that, in addition to its role in promoting MPC differentiation and fusion, Myog restricts the volume of sarcoplasm supported by each myonucleus, both in denervated (Moresi et al., 2010) and innervated (this study) adult muscle.
evidence: Stated in discussion as a conclusion from current and cited studies.

claim: Both adult mouse and zebrafish Myog mutants show reduction in Mrf4 mRNA.
source: Both adult mouse and zebrafish Myog mutants show reduction in Mrf4 mRNA (Meadows et al., 2008; Venuti et al., 1995; Knapp et al., 2006; Rawls et al., 1998; Ganassi et al., 2018).

claim: Mrf4 itself restricts murine myofibre growth.
source: Mrf4 itself restricts murine myofibre growth (Moretti et al., 2016), although no myofibre size change was reported in the various Mrf4 knockout mice (Zhang et al., 1995; Patapoutian et al., 1995).
evidence: Stated in discussion with citations.

claim: Myog may either restrict myonuclear domain size directly or by regulating Mrf4 expression.
source: So Myog may either restrict myonuclear domain size directly or by regulating Mrf4 expression.
evidence: Stated in discussion as a hypothesis.

claim: Mice do not require MuSCs to maintain adult muscle size.
source: Unlike fish, which grow to some extent throughout life, mice do not require MuSCs to maintain adult muscle size (Keefe et al., 2015).

claim: During murine adult myogenesis myonuclear accretion from MuSC-derived MPC fusion is required for myofibre growth and regeneration, as in fish.
source: Nevertheless, during murine adult myogenesis myonuclear accretion from MuSC-derived MPC fusion is required for myofibre growth and regeneration, as in fish (Pallafacchina et al., 2013).

source: Congruently, expression of fusogenic genes myomixer (mymx) and myomaker (mymk) is reduced in both myog-/- adult and embryonic muscles (Ganassi et al., 2018).

claim: Accretion of myonuclei does occur in growing myog-/- zebrafish, confirming the persistence of a Myog-independent pathway to fusion.
source: Although severely reduced, accretion of myonuclei does occur in growing myog-/- zebrafish, thus confirming the persistence of a Myog-independent pathway to fusion (Ganassi et al., 2018), which appears to allow a fraction of MPCs to sustain some muscle growth.
evidence: Stated in discussion with citation to authors' previous work.

claim: Fish lacking Myog have increased igf1 and decreased mstnb expression.
source: Fish lacking Myog have increased igf1 and decreased mstnb expression.

claim: Both igf1 increase and mstnb decrease are predicted to enhance muscle size.
source: Both changes are predicted to enhance muscle size (Gao et al., 2016; Powell-Braxton et al., 1993; Coleman et al., 1995; Durieux et al., 2007; Trendelenburg et al., 2009; Zimmers et al., 2002; McPherron et al., 1997), and both may be important in our myog mutants.
evidence: Stated in discussion with citations.

claim: Loss of Mstn increases MuSCs in amniotes.
source: As we observe in myog-/- fish, loss of Mstn increases MuSCs in amniotes (McCroskery et al., 2003; Manceau et al., 2008).

claim: MuSC contribution is dispensable for myofibre hypertrophy in Mstn knockout mice, in which growth derives from increased myonuclear domain size.
source: MuSC contribution is, however, dispensable for myofibre hypertrophy in Mstn knockout mice, in which growth derives from increased myonuclear domain size.

source: Mstn knockouts thus resemble both the MuSC increase and myofibre domain size increase in myog mutant fish.

source: Igf1 increase might thus enhance the number of MuSCs in myog mutants.

source: IGF1 and Myostatin signalling also affect MuSC activation status in mice (Cornelison and Wold, 1997; McCroskery et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2010; Chakravarthy et al., 2001) and other fish (Garikipati and Rodgers, 2012).

claim: The IGF1 signal cascade phosphorylates AKT and activates mTORC1 leading to phosphorylation of RPS6 and eIF4EBPs, with downstream effects on both MuSCs and adult myofibres.
source: The IGF1 signal cascade phosphorylates AKT and activates mTORC1 leading to phosphorylation of RPS6 and eIF4EBPs, with downstream effects on both MuSCs and adult myofibres (Schiaffino and Mammucari, 2011).

claim: No difference in Akt activation was detected in myog-/- muscle.

claim: Unaltered levels of the receptors igfr1a and igfr1b were detected in myog-/- muscle.
source: As we detected no difference in Akt activation and unaltered levels of the receptors igfr1a and igfr1b, we deduce that increased phosphorylation of RPS6 is unlikely to result from enhanced upstream IGF1 cascade.
evidence: Stated in discussion based on qPCR data.

claim: Increased phosphorylation of RPS6 is unlikely to result from enhanced upstream IGF1 cascade in myog-/- muscle.
source: As we detected no difference in Akt activation and unaltered levels of the receptors igfr1a and igfr1b, we deduce that increased phosphorylation of RPS6 is unlikely to result from enhanced upstream IGF1 cascade.
evidence: Stated in discussion as a deduction from the data.

claim: Myog-/- muscle showed significant downregulation of tsc1a and tsc1b mRNAs, that encode functional orthologues of mammalian TSC1.
source: However, myog-/- muscle showed significant downregulation of tsc1a and tsc1b mRNAs, that encode functional orthologues of mammalian TSC1, a mTORC1 inhibitor highly conserved from fly to human (DiBella et al., 2009; Nobukini and Thomas, 2004) that promotes stemness in various tissues (Chen et al., 2008; Quan et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated in discussion based on qPCR data with citations.

claim: TSC1 is a mTORC1 inhibitor highly conserved from fly to human that promotes stemness in various tissues.
source: However, myog-/- muscle showed significant downregulation of tsc1a and tsc1b mRNAs, that encode functional orthologues of mammalian TSC1, a mTORC1 inhibitor highly conserved from fly to human (DiBella et al., 2009; Nobukini and Thomas, 2004) that promotes stemness in various tissues (Chen et al., 2008; Quan et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated in discussion with citations.

claim: Mouse Tsc-/- MuSCs display enhanced pRPS6 and accelerated entry into proliferation in vivo and in vitro.
source: Mouse Tsc-/- MuSCs display enhanced pRPS6 and accelerated entry into proliferation in vivo and in vitro (Rodgers et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated in discussion with citation.

claim: Murine Myog can bind to conserved regions in Tsc1 gene, whereas Myod does not.
source: Murine Myog can bind to conserved regions in Tsc1 gene, whereas Myod does not, thus suggesting direct transcriptional regulation (Barbara Wold laboratory, Caltech; https://www.encodeproject.org/experiments/ENCSR000AID/) (ENCODE Project Consortium, 2012).
evidence: Stated in discussion with reference to ENCODE data.

claim: Loss of Myog leads to mTORC1 activation in MuSCs, exit from G0 into Galert and subsequent increase in MuSC number.
source: These observations raise the hypothesis that loss of Myog leads to mTORC1 activation in MuSCs, exit from G0 into Galert and subsequent increase in MuSC number.
evidence: Stated in discussion as a hypothesis based on the collective findings.

claim: Loss of Myog acts in adult animals to influence both MuSCs and muscle fibres, thus acting as a coordinator of tissue homeostasis.
source: Taken together, our findings suggest that loss of Myog acts in adult animals to influence both MuSCs and muscle fibres, thus acting as a coordinator of tissue homeostasis.
evidence: Stated in discussion as a conclusion from the study.
